annotationRationale: The decisive steps are simplifying adjacent squares and counting the integer solutions of the resulting inequality. Factoring instead of expanding would give the same route.

classificationReview.areaRationale: The central work is a square identity followed by a linear inequality; the counting is simply the number of integers in an interval.
classificationReview.areaCheck: The recommendation to Algebra is an obvious appropriate repair: the central work is expanding adjacent squares and solving an integer-restricted linear inequality; the counting is an interval count.

review.questionCheck: The statement, choices and key agree. Every pair corresponds uniquely to a positive integer n with difference 2n+1. The eligible values are 1 through 1011, including the endpoint difference 2023, so the answer is B.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: No additional method is needed. Factoring the same square difference or counting the resulting odd numbers gives an equivalent short calculation.
review.annotationCheck: The perfect-square formula and counting integer solutions are appropriate assessed concepts, with linear inequality solving as support. The mapping captures the positive lower endpoint and inclusive upper endpoint.
review.areaCheck: The recommendation to Algebra is an obvious appropriate repair: the central work is expanding adjacent squares and solving an integer-restricted linear inequality; the counting is an interval count.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The parameterization includes every pair exactly once. Expansion gives 2n+1≤2023, hence 1≤n≤1011. The endpoint n=1011 is allowed, n=1012 fails, and n=0 is excluded by positivity. Thus there are exactly 1011 pairs.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: LIVE and AoPS Solution 1 supply this parameterization and inequality. The candidate independently explains positivity and the one-to-one count. source-informed-original accurately describes the third-party basis.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The first move is motivated by consecutive integer square roots. Expansion, the inequality bound and the correspondence between integers and pairs are explicit. The explanation needs no additional diagram or prerequisite.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_148 is directly used in expanding (n+1)², cnm_097 in solving the linear inequality, and cnm_h020 in restricting and counting its integer solutions.
